ak_jewel_in_the_rough.blurb: A small cliff on the Turnagain Arm side of the Seward Highway south of Anchorage, sitting around 780 feet up the slope above the road. It holds five short lines, three sport and two trad, running from about 5.7 up to 5.10. The walk in is the longest part: a climb up to the Turnagain Arm Trail, a stroll south along it, then a faint path or brushy scramble to the base. This is a spot for climbers who have already worked through the busier highway walls and want something quieter with a view over the water. Expect modest height and some roughness.

ak_top_rope_boulder.blurb: A single shoreline boulder in the Capt. Cook State Recreation Area on the Kenai Peninsula, reached by walking the beach about a mile and a half from the parking area. It carries five boulder problems that start at V0 and climb to roughly V7, with a few in between, so there is something for a beginner and a couple of lines for strong boulderers. Problems range from very short to fairly tall, and some old top-rope anchors remain on the summit. Bring enough pads to feel safe on the taller faces, and plan the trip around the tide, since the beach is only walkable when the water is low.

ak_wave_boulder.blurb: One large boulder sitting in the bed of Rock Creek, in the Fairbanks and Vicinity bouldering area off the Parks Highway. It has five problems, from an easy V1 through a cluster of V4 and V5 lines to one V7, so it suits climbers who want a focused session at a mid to hard level rather than a big circuit. Getting here takes a real hike up the creek, roughly three quarters of an hour or more, and the boulder lies on the right side of the stream bed. Water in the creek tends to dry up toward fall, which makes the walk easier later in the season.
ak_wave_boulder.parking_note: Leave the car at the pull-out beside the Parks Highway near mile 261, between markers 261 and 262, then head north toward the creek.

ak_far_out.blurb: A small cluster of boulders along Sheep Creek near Nenana, in the Fairbanks and Vicinity region, at around 1,900 feet. Five problems are described here, all in the V2 to V5 range, with two at V2, two at V3 and a single harder one, so it works best for climbers warming into moderate bouldering. The boulders sit a short walk upstream from the neighboring Marbless area, and a few more small blocs lie further up the creek. The creek is reached by walking the railroad corridor south from the Nenana Bridge to a trestle, so expect an outing of some distance before you even start climbing.

ak_first_rock_2.blurb: The first formation you meet on the Angel Rocks trail in the Angel Creek Rocks area, off Chena Hot Springs Road near Fairbanks. It is a small granite outcrop, open and mostly sunny, with five short lines at easy to moderate grades, roughly 5.5 up to 5.8. Most can be led on trad gear or set up as top-ropes, and one is top-rope only. That makes it a reasonable place for beginners or for a quick warm-up before heading to the bigger rocks nearby. The walk in is about half an hour or less along the trail, which hikers also use, so the cliff sees casual foot traffic.

ak_canwell_crag.blurb: A short cliff high in the Delta Range, east of the Delta River off the Richardson Highway, sitting near 3,600 feet below Canwell Peak above a small alpine lake. Five crack lines make up the crag, mostly trad or top-rope, plus one sport route, running from easy 5.7 terrain up past 5.11. The cracks reward a range of jamming techniques, and the rock is clean but only lightly brushed, so a few placements may need care with moisture and moss. The face stays in shade, so snow lingers into late spring or early summer and autumn is the suggested time to come. The approach takes about half an hour.
